_meta.title: AI Challenge of the Week
_meta.rotationNote: Rotation by ISO calendar week; after week 12 it restarts at week 1. The next twelve challenges are prepared by week 10.

challenges.role: HR lead at an 80-person engineering company
challenges.scenario: The CFO wants a salary benchmark against five competitors in three days. You have public sources such as company reports, job listings and employee-submitted salary data, two hours for the first analysis and no data analyst. How do you get to a defensible draft?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Write the brief with role, company, region and five columns: competitor, role and level, reported salary range, source, confidence. 2. Collect a few documented public records per competitor, respect site terms and never present estimates as payroll facts. 3. Have the model extract the ranges and mark uncertain or missing values. 4. Check the three most critical claims at the original sources. 5. Record the sample limits and deliver the reviewed table.
rubric: The brief states role, context and output format
Named public sources replace an undefined web search
Sample sizes and source limits are recorded
Uncertain values carry a confidence label
A critical review happens before delivery
The format matches the table the CFO needs
The two hours cover a bounded first analysis, not a full compensation study

challenges.role: Sales lead at a 45-person trade business
challenges.scenario: 230 open quotations in the system, some 90 days old. Nobody knows which are still live. Checking them all by hand takes an estimated three days. How do you build a review queue in two hours?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Export only customer reference, value, last activity and status; personal data runs through the approved process. 2. Define review classes such as HOT, WARM, COLD and DEAD with fixed age and value thresholds. 3. Have follow-up drafts written for a person to approve; nothing goes out automatically. 4. The top records get a personal call and the rest go into review queues. Never archive on a model rating alone. 5. Compare the rules with actual outcomes every week.
rubric: Data is exported, not retyped
Triage classes use named, reviewable thresholds
Each class has a draft in plain business language
A person reviews every high-value follow-up
Two hours cover triage setup and drafts
A recurring review replaces a one-off cleanup
Customer data runs only through an approved data-protection and access path

challenges.scenario: The monthly report covers eight metrics, four departments and twelve commentary lines and has taken six hours so far. Today a colleague is out and you have 90 minutes. How do you get to a reviewable draft?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Set up a controlled workspace with the last three reports as structure and style reference. 2. Add the current raw figures as a validated table. 3. Ask for the same structure, stated variance calculations and commentary that separates fact from hypothesis. 4. Recalculate every figure in Excel and check the source cell. 5. Investigate two or three material variances and note several possible explanations instead of one unevidenced cause. 6. Export the reviewed document in the required format.
rubric: Previous reports serve as structure and style reference
Every figure is checked independently of generated prose
Variance rules are fixed before the draft
Possible explanations are marked as hypotheses
Checking gets more time than wording
The final format matches management's reporting
Workspace and checks are reusable next month

challenges.role: Executive assistant at a 200-person software company
challenges.scenario: Tomorrow morning an executive flies to an investor meeting. By tonight you need an eight-page briefing on three competitors, covering public financial information, product positioning, management, recent announcements and an evidence-based risk assessment.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Fix the eight pages before any research: one summary, two per competitor, one comparison. 2. Collect the same source categories for each competitor, with date and direct link. 3. Have a draft written against the template with every uncertain statement marked. 4. Check financial figures and quotations in the original documents. 5. Compare on financial strength, delivery pace, team and product, and back every rating. 6. Deliver the reviewed briefing and a one-page meeting reference.
rubric: The structure is fixed before drafting
Every competitor follows the same source plan
The writing follows an approved internal example rather than consulting language
Financial figures and quotations are checked at the source
The comparison matrix separates evidence from judgement
The deliverables are the briefing and a short meeting reference
The four-hour plan limits scope and reserves time for checking

challenges.role: IT lead at a 60-person family business
challenges.scenario: Management asks where AI would be worth it and wants a first concept next week. The budget is open, time is short and the company has no AI practice yet. Where do you start?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1: list candidate use cases for the industry and strike every one without a clear process owner or data path. 2. Day 2: ask eight people from different functions five short questions about recurring work and failure points. Have the model cluster the answers and check each cluster against the originals. 3. Day 3: compare the remaining cases on effort, staff affected, data sensitivity, operational risk and time to evidence. 4. Put forward two candidates with assumptions, exclusions, controls and the next validation step. State any benefit as a range built from named inputs, never as a promise.
rubric: External research is combined with employee evidence
The model helps cluster but does not decide
Effort, reach, risk and time to evidence are criteria
Management gets two prioritised candidates, not a long list
The output fits on one decision page
Each candidate has a validation step and an owner
Three days leave time to check sources

challenges.role: Marketing lead at a 30-person B2B software company
challenges.scenario: You are planning the Q3 LinkedIn calendar with three posts a week for 13 weeks on AI-native teams. There is no agency budget, and nobody but you works on it.
challenges.timeBudget: 1 day for the Q3 plan plus 30 minutes per week for drafting
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Analyse the last 30 posts and their performance data and derive three repeatable formats; small samples prove no causation. 2. Have topics proposed for a German B2B audience and pick 39 without duplicates. 3. Fix each topic's angle and the evidence it needs before any hook or call to action. 4. The quarterly calendar names owner, source status and review date. 5. Write three drafts a week and edit them for factual accuracy and company voice. 6. Review performance monthly and note what you change.
rubric: Earlier posts shape the style without being copied
Performance data informs selection, with its limits recorded
The calendar has exactly 39 topics for 3 posts across 13 weeks
An angle and evidence requirement precede each draft
The weekly 30 minutes cover drafting; review time comes on top
A monthly review forms a documented feedback loop
The language is precise and suits a German B2B audience

challenges.scenario: Customers have asked for three competing features, and the next sprint has room for one. How do you decide, and how do you document the decision?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Record each request with customer context and usage data. 2. Note each feature's user problem, affected segments and existing substitutes. 3. Build a RICE table with written definitions for reach, impact, confidence and effort. The model calculates only once the inputs are checked. 4. Plan one small research step for each thinly evidenced estimate. 5. Record decision, assumptions and rejected alternatives. 6. After release, compare actual use and outcomes with the estimates.
rubric: A defined method replaces an undocumented preference
Product-usage evidence is included
Confidence is explicit and tied to evidence
Thin-evidence assumptions get a research action
The decision and rejected alternatives are recorded
A post-release measurement point is defined
The model structures and calculates; the accountable owner decides

challenges.role: Compliance officer at a medium-sized financial company
challenges.scenario: Management wants an AI chat assistant in customer advice. Within two weeks you must justify whether the plan can proceed and under which conditions. GDPR, the EU AI Act and sector rules can all apply at once.
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Describe the system, user journey, decision effects, data categories, model provider and human role. 2. Check each legal framework separately against primary sources: GDPR legal basis, minimisation and DPIA; role and risk class under the EU AI Act; applicable financial-supervision requirements. 3. Build a traceable list of requirements, evidence and open questions. 4. Qualified legal and compliance owners review the analysis. 5. Build a decision matrix with permitted scope, prohibited uses, contracts, controls, tests and training. 6. Record the recommendation and its conditions; model output is not legal advice.
rubric: GDPR, the EU AI Act and sector rules are checked separately
Primary sources support the summary
A qualified legal or compliance review is mandatory
The matrix separates permitted scope, exclusions and conditions
Required evidence such as contracts, assessments and training records is named
Management gets a conditional recommendation, not a binary model answer
Risk class and assessment decisions are documented for later audit

challenges.role: HR lead at a 500-person industrial company
challenges.scenario: 370 applications in ten days for five vacancies. The team manages 20 a day and needs a lawful triage process by Friday. How do you cut the administrative work without handing employment decisions to a model?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Before any model is used, the hiring owners set measurable requirements, evidence rules and prohibited proxy criteria per role. 2. Confirm legal basis, retention, access rights, provider contract, EU AI Act classification and required impact assessments. 3. Use AI only for approved admin work, such as pulling evidence into a review table. Applications are never ranked or rejected automatically. 4. Recruiters read the source application and decide every case. 5. Test for extraction errors and disparate outcomes, edge cases included. 6. Keep an audit trail and give applicants the required information and rights process.
rubric: Job criteria and prohibited proxies are fixed beforehand
Legal basis, EU AI Act classification and impact assessments are checked
The model never ranks or rejects on its own
A recruiter checks source evidence and decides every case
Accuracy and bias tests include documented edge cases
Retention, access and applicant-rights processes are recorded
The output is a review table with sources, not an unexplained score

challenges.role: Sales engineer at an enterprise B2B software company
challenges.scenario: An enterprise customer wants a technical proof of concept with your system and access to its database in ten days. Work like this normally takes six weeks. Do you accept, and with what scope and controls?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1: search the internal repository for comparable proofs of concept and record reusable components with licence, owner and test state. 2. Days 1 and 2: agree five observable user stories, a data-access boundary, acceptance criteria and exclusions. 3. Days 3 to 7: build and test in an isolated environment and review the generated code and dependencies. 4. Day 8: internal security and operations review of authentication, audit logs, rate limits, secrets and teardown. 5. Day 9: rehearse the demonstration and the failure path. 6. Day 10: show the agreed scope and record what production would still need.
rubric: Existing components are checked for reuse, not assumed
Scope is limited to five observable user stories
A person reviews the generated code and tests
Authentication, audit logs, rate limits, secrets and teardown are checked
An internal dry run precedes the customer session
The proof of concept is clearly separate from a production commitment
The ten-day plan names owners, review gates and exclusions

challenges.role: Office manager at a 40-person law firm
challenges.scenario: The firm gets 120 client emails a day: 40 percent on existing matters, 30 percent appointments, 20 percent new enquiries and 10 percent spam or sales. Two people cannot keep up. How do you cut the work without exposing privileged information or sending unreviewed legal communications?
challenges.timeBudget: 1 week for setup plus continuous improvement
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Before choosing a model, settle what confidentiality, professional secrecy, retention and access require. Local execution can reduce transfers but alone proves no compliance. 2. Build an isolated n8n workflow that sorts example or approved messages into four queues. 3. Appointment and acknowledgement messages stay drafts until authorised staff release them. 4. Existing-matter and ambiguous messages go to the responsible team without generated legal advice. 5. Keep spam handling reversible during evaluation. 6. Review classification errors weekly and update the fixed test set first. 7. Document the assessment, provider and processor roles, staff procedure and client information duties with qualified counsel.
rubric: The architecture follows confidentiality and professional secrecy
Classification routes messages and makes no legal decisions
Authorised staff release every template before sending
Ambiguous messages and existing matters have a fixed path
A weekly error review updates a fixed test set
The legal assessment and data-protection controls are documented
Qualified counsel assesses client transparency duties

challenges.scenario: Planning for 2027 fills 200 spreadsheet rows across targets, budget and team growth. It used to take two weeks. You want two days without lowering the review standard. How do you cut the work down?
challenges.modelSolution: 1. Day 1, morning: compare the last three plans with actual results and find the categories with repeated forecast error. 2. Day 1, afternoon: record the 2027 assumptions with source, owner and confidence, then build a base, a downside and an upside scenario. 3. Day 2, morning: functional leads challenge the assumptions and open risks are written down. The model can structure the discussion but cannot validate a business assumption. 4. Day 2, afternoon: finish the controlled workbook and a one-page summary per scenario. 5. Schedule quarterly plan-to-actual checks. Two days is a bounded process target and does not guarantee equal quality.
rubric: Earlier plan-to-actual gaps feed calibration
Base, downside and upside scenarios use stated assumptions
Functional leads challenge the assumptions
Each scenario has a one-page decision summary
Quarterly reviews compare actuals with the plan
The model structures; the managing director stays accountable
The two-day target keeps fixed verification and sign-off gates
